extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political philosophy, educators, and poets concerned with literature for civic education
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for what stories, poems, and portrayals are appropriate for educating guardian-citizens in an ideal State; includes selection/censorship rules, desired moral/psychological effects, and the physical and moral qualities required of guardians. Applicable to composing or evaluating literature intended for formative civic education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Censorship of storytellers
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish a censorship of the writers of fiction: the censors receive any tale of fiction which is good, and reject the bad; mothers and nurses must tell children only the authorised tales; most tales in current use must be discarded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Founders of a State should determine the general forms and limits for poets; the censors must fashion the minds of the young by selecting tales that form virtuous character. This is procedural: create a system to vet and authorise stories for youth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin education with music and literature
rubrics_metrics.description: Education has two divisions—gymnastic for the body and music for the soul—and instruction should begin with music (including literature) before gymnastic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The beginning is the most important part of any work; early tales leave indelible impressions on character, so musical/literary instruction for the young should be carefully controlled to form desired dispositions prior to physical training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Represent the gods as truly good (God is cause of good only)
rubrics_metrics.description: God is always to be represented as he truly is — good — and must not be represented as the author of evils; 'God is not the author of all things, but of good only.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poets must not assert that gods dispense good and evil alike (reject lines like 'two casks lie at the threshold of Zeus, one of good, the other of evil'). If poets must mention divine-caused punishment, they must frame it so that God does what is just and the punished are worse off for their wickedness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forbid portrayals of gods as shape-shifters or deceivers
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not represent gods as magicians who appear in many shapes, transform themselves, or deceive men; gods are unchangeable and incapable of falsehood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prohibit myths that present gods disguising themselves or using deception (e.g., Proteus/Thetis disguises). Such representations make children cowardly or blasphemous and misrepresent divine nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude myths of quarrelling, immoral, or cruel divine behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not tell children tales that present quarrels, plots, fights, or immoral conduct among gods and heroes (e.g., the wars in heaven, Cronus's deeds, Hephaestus binding Hera).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These stories are 'bad lies' and set corrupt examples; if mention is absolutely necessary, restrict to mystery rites with very few initiated and avoid ordinary instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expunge depictions making the afterlife terrifying
rubrics_metrics.description: Remove passages that portray the world below (Hades) as grim, squalid, full of sapless shades, Cocytus, Styx, ghosts, etc., because they make death seem awful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such poetical charms are especially unfit for guardians and the young, since fear of death undermines courage; replace with nobler strains that do not render guardians effeminate or excitable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remove lamentations and excessive mourning from tales
rubrics_metrics.description: Reject the weepings and wailings of famous men and make lamentation the province of women or men of baser sort; guardians should be trained not to indulge in excessive mourning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good man, being sufficient for himself, should not view death as terrible and therefore should not be taught to lament; doing so preserves courage and equanimity among defenders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibit representations of gods or heroes overcome by excessive laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not admit depictions where persons of worth — and especially gods — are represented as overcome by laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excessive laughter produces violent reaction; guardians should not be taught to be given to laughter, nor should the gods be misrepresented in this way.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrict lying: truth valued, lying only for rulers for public good
rubrics_metrics.description: Truth is highly valued; lying is hateful in highest matters. The privilege of lying should be reserved to the rulers, permitted only for the public good; all other lying is punishable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lies may be used as a 'medicine' by rulers in dealings with enemies or for public benefit, analogous to a physician's use of remedies. Private citizens lying is subversive and should be punished (e.g., craftsmen, priests, physicians).

rubrics_metrics.name: Select guardians by bodily qualities (speed, strength, swiftness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Guardians must be quick to see, swift to overtake the enemy, and strong — bodily qualities necessary for watching and defending the city.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are basic physical prerequisites for the role; selection of natures fitted by nature for guarding is a duty of founders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select guardians by spirited character (thumos) — bravery and spirit
rubrics_metrics.description: Guardians must possess spirit (thumos): the quality that makes the soul fearless and indomitable, which is essential for bravery in battle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spirit alone can make a man brave; without it he will not fight well. But spirit must be balanced (see also gentleness to friends) to avoid internal savagery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require guardians to combine spirit with gentleness and self-restraint
rubrics_metrics.description: Guardians must be dangerous to enemies and gentle to friends — a combination of spiritedness and gentleness (self-control), not savagery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Though spirit tends toward savagery, exemplars in nature (dogs) show this combination is possible; selection must seek natures that unite these opposites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require guardians to be lovers of learning (philosophical disposition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A guardian should unite philosophy and spirit — being a lover of wisdom so that his likes and dislikes are determined by knowledge rather than mere impulse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The analogy of the dog: distinguishing friend and enemy by knowledge. Thus a guardian with philosophical bent will be gentle to friends and hostile to enemies appropriately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education regimen for guardians: music (soul) then gymnastic (body)
rubrics_metrics.description: Guardians' rearing and education should begin with music (including properly censored literature) to shape the soul, followed later by gymnastic training for the body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This ordered education illuminates how justice and injustice grow in States and serves the larger end of creating just guardians; stories used in musical instruction must be the authorised, virtuous tales.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approve literature that fosters temperance and obedience
rubrics_metrics.description: Youth must be temperate; chief elements of temperance are obedience to commanders and self-control in sensual pleasures. Approve language and verses that express obedience and silent awe of leaders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject impertinent lines that show private individuals addressing rulers with disrespect (examples cited). Cultural texts should cultivate obedience and self-restraint among guardians.
